extracted.intended_audience: film historians, students, and general readers interested in censorship and film history
extracted.subtask_short: films condemned by Legion of Decency
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological/list article documenting films the U.S. National Legion of Decency rated 'C' (Condemned), with background on the organization's rating system, the grounds cited for condemnation, and its policies and practices toward revisions and enforcement. Useful for researching reasons films were deemed morally offensive and how the Legion operated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legion rating system (A/B/C) and historical change to O
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legion rated films according to suitability with codes A, B, or C; C was identified as 'Condemned' for viewing by Catholics. The C rating was issued from 1933 until 1978. In 1978 the rating system was revised and the designation 'condemned' was not assigned thereafter; films previously rated C or B were rated O ('morally offensive').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes NCOMP (National Catholic Office for Motion Pictures) reassigned ratings to old films under the new system (making it impossible to tell whether a film now classified O had originally been B or C). Also: NCOMP ceased operations in 1980. The Legion's ratings applied to U.S. and imported films and were issued when films were released for distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemned (C) = morally offensive / unsuitable for Catholics
rubrics_metrics.description: A film given the C rating was identified as 'Condemned' for viewing by Catholics — i.e., judged morally offensive or unsuitable for Catholic audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being placed on the condemned list could trigger Legion-organized boycotts that harmed a film's distribution and profitability. Studios sometimes edited films to avoid a C rating; the Legion sometimes revised a C to B after changes, while at other times it refused to remove an original rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual content / nudity / explicit sexual material
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for sexual content including nudity, explicit sexual content, 'pornographic in intent', 'suggestive costumes', and 'suggestive situations and costuming.' Specific citations include rulings that a film was 'too shocking and almost pornographic', or that 'nudity has been used.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Pawnbroker was condemned 'for the sole reason that nudity has been used.' Barbarella and Blowup were condemned for nudity/explicit sexual content. Studios frequently removed or cut scenes (e.g., 15 minutes cut from The Blue Lagoon) to satisfy the Legion and earn a lesser rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child exploitation / underage sexual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for material involving minors, e.g., 'child pornography' concerns and depictions of underage marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretty Baby is noted as condemned due to child pornography concerns; Child Bride (presented under 'Dust to Dust') is listed as an exploitation film about underage marriage. Such issues were cited as grounds for condemnation and severe public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity, indecency, and foul language
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemnations were issued for 'grossly obscene, suggestive and indecent action, costuming and dialogue' and for use of foul language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ice Castles and Dawn of the Dead are mentioned among the last films condemned for foul language and abuse. The Legion's language could emphasize potential 'grave, evil influence' especially on youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blasphemy / irreverent or disrespectful treatment of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for irreverent or blasphemous treatment of religious practices or for being 'religiously insensitive' or misrepresenting Christian doctrine/eschatology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example quotes: César condemned for 'Irreverent and blasphemous treatment of religious practices.' The Omen was condemned for misrepresenting Christian eschatology. Such religious concerns were explicit grounds for C ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic portrayal of illicit or immoral actions; vice portrayed attractively
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned when vice or illicit behavior was portrayed attractively or when virtue was ridiculed — e.g., 'Vice is portrayed attractively; virtue ridiculed' and 'sympathetic portrayal of illicit actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Legion objected to narratives that seemed to justify or glamorize criminality, prostitution, or other illicit behavior, listing these portrayals as reasons for condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: General atmosphere of sordidness or moral ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemnation could be based on a film's 'general atmosphere of sordidness and abnormality' or development 'in an atmosphere of complete moral ambiguity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Jour Se Lève and L'Avventura were condemned in part for their overall sordid or morally ambiguous tone rather than a single explicit scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence, cruelty, and degrading scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for scenes of cruelty deemed 'degrading and corruptive' or for 'sheer animalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baby Doll was described as 'morally repellent both in theme and treatment' with 'scenes of cruelty are degrading and corruptive.' Such language was used to justify condemnation on grounds of violent or degrading content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitative or pseudo-documentary presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Films purporting to be documentaries or educational but presented in an exploitative manner (e.g., nudist colony films, sexploitation pseudo-documentaries) were condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jungle Stampede 'purports to be a documentary and educational in nature' but was condemned for its handling of native customs; numerous exploitation films and 'nudist colony' pictures were listed among condemned titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of marriage, sexuality, and family values (including contraception/assisted reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for 'an immoral and un-Christian attitude toward marriage and its obligations' or for 'justifying artificial insemination' or 'endorsing birth control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encompassed objections to plots or attitudes that the Legion judged hostile to traditional Christian views of marriage and family (e.g., This Thing Called Love initially condemned; A Question of Adultery condemned for justifying artificial insemination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological or political objections (e.g., perceived Marxian propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Films were condemned for ideological reasons, such as being 'an ideological perversion of the subject to purposes of Marxian Communism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time in the Sun was called out for an account of Mexican history that the Legion labeled as ideological perversion to Marxian Communism — showing the Legion sometimes judged films on political/ideological content as well as moral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/rating policies: timing, reassessment, and refusal to reconsider
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legion reviewed films when released for distribution (often rating non-U.S. films years after their original release). It sometimes revised ratings after studios made cuts; at other times it refused to remove original ratings. By 1962 the Legion adopted a policy of not reconsidering a film's rating once it was widely distributed (with some exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studios used edits, added prologues, or apologized publicly to avoid or reverse a C rating (e.g., The Seven Year Itch, A Streetcar Named Desire, Forever Amber). The 1978 revision of the system (to O) and NCOMP's reassignment of old ratings are also procedural points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement tactics and industry impact (boycotts and pressure to self-censor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legion organized boycotts and used the threat of a C rating to pressure studios into revisions; such measures could damage a film's distribution and profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the Legion sometimes preferred to keep an original C rating to avoid publicity from a downgrade, producing industry self-censorship. Examples include studio edits made to avoid a C and instances where the Legion's actions led to cuts or distribution delays (e.g., The Outlaw, Forever Amber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on reporting: not all films 'reported condemned' actually received a C rating
rubrics_metrics.description: The page warns that films are often reported to have been 'condemned' in general terms when they did not receive the Legion's C rating; some festival programs or older lists mix films condemned by other local Catholic lists with Legion C ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Turner Classic Movies programmed a festival 'Movies Condemned by the Catholic Legion of Decency' that included several films not rated C by the Legion. Early Chicago Archdiocese lists are sometimes misattributed to the Legion.
